| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-06 | semantics | core | EXIT HANDLER re-raises the current exception into the lexical environment surrounding the innermost protection block, so handling proceeds as if the handler did not exist, apart from statements already executed inside it. | EXC-0032 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-07 | semantics | core | Reaching the USE line of a when-use block, the END WHEN of a when-use-name block, or the END HANDLER of a detached handler resumes execution at the line after the corresponding END WHEN; reaching a detached HANDLER line without an exception resumes at the line right after its END HANDLER. | EXC-0033 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-08 | semantics | core | CAUSE EXCEPTION raises a fatal exception and sets EXTYPE to the rounded value of its exception-type argument (the exception listed for a cause-statement in section 12.1.5). | EXC-0034, EXC-0035, EXC-0260, EXC-0261 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-09 | semantics | core | An exception raised by a statement sitting inside an exception handler is not caught by that handler; it is handled by the default exception-handling procedures. | EXC-0036, EXC-0083 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-10 | semantics | core | A fatal exception in a procedure that no enclosing WHEN block catches propagates back to the line that invoked the procedure, and keeps propagating until a handler resolves it or the main program applies the default procedures. | EXC-0037 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-11 | semantics | core | When a handler is entered because of such propagation, EXTYPE returns 100000 plus the value it would have had where the exception first arose, and EXLINE returns the number of the most recent line the exception was propagated to. | EXC-0038, EXC-0079 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-12 | semantics | core | The default exception handling always reports the EXTYPE and EXLINE of the original exception. | EXC-0039 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-13 | semantics | core | EXTYPE values for exceptions defined by local enhancements are negative, and when such a negative value is propagated it becomes -100000 plus the value for the original exception. | EXC-0040, EXC-0080 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-14 | semantics | core | EXTYPE values from 1 to 999 are reserved: neither future revisions of the standard nor local enhancements may assign them. | EXC-0041 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-15 | semantics | core | EXTEXT$ with a numeric argument returns the system message text for the exception number obtained by rounding the argument, and returns the null string when that number is not a standard system exception. | EXC-0042, EXC-0100, EXC-0101 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-16 | semantics | core | If the exception propagates all the way to the main program without any handler being invoked there, the default handling procedures of the standard apply. | EXC-0043 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-17 | semantics | core | Inside a WHEN block, a PRINT USING whose value overflows its format-item (nonfatal 8203, or 8204 for the exrad) emits nothing for the failing field: no asterisk fill and no unformatted value on the next line, because those are the default recovery procedures of 10.4.5, which do not apply when a programmer handler exists; values preceding the failing one in the same statement were already generated (10.4.4.2) and remain on the current line, and no final end-of-line is generated (10.4.4.5) since generation did not complete. | EXC-0064, EXC-0065, EXC-0066 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-18 | semantics | core | Inside a WHEN block, a PRINT to a file with USING that raises 8203/8204 adds no record to the file at all (not even a partial one, and not even for values preceding the failing one in the same statement), because an exception during data transfer never adds a partial file element (11.3.4) and an exception before completion of the statement adds no record (11.3.4.1). | EXC-0068 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-19 | semantics | core | Inside a WHEN block, a USING$ call that raises 8203/8204 (the 10.4.5 exceptions apply to USING$ per 6.4.4) is aborted without producing a value: the destination variable keeps its previous value, since the asterisk-filled string is the default recovery, not the function's result. | EXC-0067 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-20 | semantics | core | Inside a WHEN block, a GRAPH TEXT with USING that raises 8203/8204 draws nothing: the asterisk-filled text is the default recovery of 10.4.5, which does not apply when a programmer handler exists. | GFX-0139 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-CL13 | semantics | core | An exception raised in a GOSUB or ON GOSUB subroutine called from inside a when-block is not propagated, because a GOSUB subroutine is part of the same block and not a procedure-part or an internal-proc-def: the handler sees the original EXTYPE (3001 for a division by zero), without 100000 added, and EXLINE is the line whose execution caused the exception. RETRY and CONTINUE in that handler resume inside the subroutine (the line again, or the next one) and its RETURN returns after the GOSUB; a handler that ends at END WHEN or EXIT HANDLER leaves no GOSUB frame pending. Procedure-parts and internal-proc-defs (SUB, FUNCTION, DEF, PICTURE) still add 100000 once, or -100000 for a negative EXTYPE. | EXC-0244, EXC-0245, EXC-0246, EXC-0247, EXC-0248, EXC-0249, EXC-0250, EXC-0251, EXC-0252, EXC-0253, EXC-0254, EXC-0255, EXC-0256, EXC-0257, EXC-0258, EXC-0259 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-TR128 | semantics | core | A detached-handler of an EXTERNAL SUB, FUNCTION or PICTURE is part of that program unit and behaves as an exception-handler in its when-use-block: it sees and assigns the parameters of the unit (numeric, string and array, by reference), a function-let in it gives the value of the FUNCTION, and RESTORE n in it may name a DATA line of the unit; a RESTORE n that names a DATA line of another program unit is rejected before the program runs. | PRT-0314, PRT-0315, SEG-0501, SEG-0502, SEG-0503 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-TR130 | semantics | core | A detached-handler is part of the program unit that contains it: in an EXTERNAL unit its variables are variables of that unit, even when the unit has no parameters (not those of the main program or of another unit); the handler of an internal SUB or FUNCTION sees the parameters of the routine and of its unit, and a function-let in it is a function-let of the FUNCTION, which for an EXTERNAL or internal FUNCTION may be its only one; an IMAGE line or a DIM in the handler of an EXTERNAL unit belongs to that unit and may be used by its body. | SEG-0504, SEG-0505, SEG-0506, SEG-0507, PRT-0316, ARR-0316 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-TR131 | semantics | core | EXIT SUB in an exception-handler of a SUB (in-line use-part or detached handler, EXTERNAL or internal SUB) ends the invocation of the SUB: the separate GOSUB stack of the handler is only for RETURN, and EXIT SUB is not a RETURN. When a handler calls a routine that handles an exception of its own, EXTYPE and EXLINE (and the GOSUB stack) of the calling handler are those of the exception that made it run, when control comes back to it. | SEG-0508, SEG-0509, SEG-0510, EXC-0211, EXC-0212, EXC-0213 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-TR133 | semantics | core | An EXIT PICTURE in a detached-handler of a PICTURE (EXTERNAL, or internal to the main program or to an EXTERNAL unit) occurs within the picture-def, since the handler is part of the program unit that contains it, and ends the picture. In the detached-handler of a SUB or of the main program it is still rejected. | GFX-0187, GFX-0188 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-TR143 | semantics | core | The detached-handler of the main program, and that of an internal SUB or FUNCTION of the main program, sees the arrays that the main program declares with DIM, numeric and string, and may read and assign their elements, as the USE part of the when-block does. | ARR-0370, ARR-0371 |
| 12.1.4 | A-12.1.4-TR151 | semantics | core | A detached-handler whose exception-handler is empty (no lines, or only a REM line) is valid: when the exception is handled by it, execution continues with the line that follows the block that raised the exception (after its END WHEN), in the main program, in an internal or EXTERNAL SUB and in a FUNCTION, whether the exception is raised by CAUSE EXCEPTION or by a run-time error. | EXC-0230, EXC-0231, EXC-0232, EXC-0233, EXC-0234 |
| 12.1.6 | A-12.1.6-01 | semantics | core | A nonfatal exception raised inside a procedure called from a when-block is not passed back to the calling routine: it is handled by an exception handler in the called routine if there is one, otherwise by the system handler, which reports it at the line where it occurred and lets the called routine continue. | EXC-0077, EXC-0078 |
| 12.2.3 | A-12.2.3-EX | syntax | core | Both forms shown in the examples of section 12.2.3, plain TRACE ON and TRACE ON TO #3, are accepted. | EXC-0044 |
| 12.2.3 | A-ECMA-36 | syntax | core | TRACE ON and TRACE ON TO a display file are accepted and can be switched off again. | ECMA-0093, ECMA-0094 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-01 | semantics | core | Every program unit (the main program or a procedure; an internal SUB, FUNCTION or handler is not one) carries a debugging status (active or inactive) of its own: inactive for all units at program start, persisting across invocations of that unit except in the main program, and changing one unit's status never affects another unit. | EXC-0045 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-02 | semantics | core | DEBUG ON activates debugging and DEBUG OFF deactivates it for the program unit containing the statement, lasting for the rest of that invocation and every later invocation of that unit until the opposite statement runs there. | EXC-0046 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-03 | semantics | core | Executing BREAK while debugging is active raises an exception whose standard recovery reports the line number of the BREAK and tells the user that debugger interaction is possible. | EXC-0047 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-04 | semantics | core | Executing BREAK while debugging is inactive has no effect; execution simply moves on to the next line. | EXC-0048 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-05 | semantics | core | With debugging active, TRACE ON and TRACE OFF switch tracing on or off in the program unit containing the statement; tracing is off at each entry to a program unit (an external procedure, not an internal SUB or FUNCTION), and with debugging inactive a TRACE statement has no effect. | EXC-0049, EXC-0050 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-06 | semantics | core | Running a TRACE statement never changes the debugging status, and running a DEBUG statement never changes the tracing status. | EXC-0051 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-07 | semantics | core | While tracing is on and debugging active, every executed line that interrupts the sequential flow reports its own line number and that of the next line to run, and every line assigning to a variable or array element reports its line number together with the values assigned. | EXC-0052 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-08 | semantics | core | Trace reports are written to the display-format file on the channel named in TRACE ... TO, or to the device of channel zero when no channel is named. | EXC-0053 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-09 | semantics | core | Every trace report at least shows the traced variable's name as it appears in the statement plus its value, and for an array element the subscript values as well. | EXC-0054 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-TR102 | semantics | core | With tracing on, a line whose execution raises an exception that transfers control to an exception-handler is reported together with the first line of the handler as the next line to be executed, for a handler in line and for a detached handler; the use-line and the handler-line are not executed and are not reported. | EXC-0206 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-TR111 | semantics | core | With tracing on, an exception raised in an external procedure without debugging and handled by the exception-handler of the calling unit is reported by the calling unit as the line of its CALL together with the first line of the handler; and when the first line of the handler is a remark-line, that line is reported as the next line to be executed, for a handler in line and for a detached handler. | EXC-0207, EXC-0208 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-TR120 | semantics | core | With tracing on, an exception raised in an external procedure without debugging and propagated out of it by EXIT HANDLER to the exception-handler of the calling unit is reported by the calling unit as the line of its CALL together with the first line of the handler. | EXC-0209 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-TR125 | semantics | core | With tracing on, the line of an EXIT HANDLER that passes control to another exception-handler (the enclosing WHEN of the same unit, or the handler of the calling unit) is reported together with the first line of that handler, not with its use-line or handler-line, which is not executed. | EXC-0210 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-TR134 | semantics | core | When a line that assigns a value to a formal parameter of a SUB (by reference, with a literal argument, in an internal or an EXTERNAL SUB, or in its detached-handler) is traced, the report includes the name of the parameter and the value assigned, as for any other variable. | EXC-0214, EXC-0215, EXC-0216 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-TR136 | semantics | core | When a line that assigns a value to an element of an array that is a formal parameter of a SUB (a vector or a matrix, in an internal or an EXTERNAL SUB), or that assigns to the whole formal-array with MAT, is traced, the report includes the name of the formal-array, the subscripts and the value of each element assigned, as for a local array. | EXC-0217, EXC-0218, EXC-0219, EXC-0220 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-TR161 | semantics | core | When line-numbers are repeated between program-units (4.2.2), the trace identifies a line by its program-unit: the transfer from the END SUB of line 40 of an external unit to line 40 of the calling program is reported (40 -> 40) and the line that follows it is traced, and the report of a line shows the text of that line in its own unit, not that of a line with the same number in another unit. | EXC-0240, EXC-0241, EXC-0242, EXC-0243 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-TR88A | semantics | core | An internal SUB, an internal FUNCTION and a handler are not program units (a program unit is a main program or a procedure; internal procedure definitions lie inside the unit that contains them), so they share the debugging and tracing status of that unit and the lines of their bodies, and the use-part of a handler, are traced like any other line of the unit. | EXC-0102 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-TR88B | semantics | core | GOSUB, ON GOSUB and RETURN do not change the program unit, so tracing stays on after them: the subroutine lines, the line after the GOSUB and every later line are reported, and the RETURN line reports the line it returns to. | EXC-0103 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-TR88C | semantics | core | With tracing on, the lines CALL (to the first line of the SUB body), END SUB (to the line after the CALL), EXIT DO (to the line after the loop-line), LOOP (back to the do-line) and EXIT FOR (to the line after the next-line) are lines that interrupt the sequential order and report their own line number and that of the next line to be executed; so does the exit of a DO WHILE or DO UNTIL. | EXC-0104 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-TR88D | semantics | core | With tracing on, a line that assigns values reports them whatever the statement: MAT INPUT, LINE INPUT, MAT READ, an array assignment (all the new elements) and a LET inside an external SUB, as well as LET, INPUT, READ and FOR. | EXC-0105 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-TR95A | semantics | core | With tracing on, the use-line of a when-use-block reached without an exception reports itself and the line after the protection-block, and the end-handler-line of a detached handler reports itself and the line after the end-when-line of the block that raised the exception; the end-when-lines that are not executed, and the use-part of a block that did not raise, are not reported, and the when-line is reported once. | EXC-0132 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-TR95B | semantics | core | With tracing on, an internal SUB or FUNCTION line reached in the sequence of lines reports itself and the line after its END SUB or END FUNCTION, which is the next line to be executed; the body, which is not executed, is not reported. | EXC-0133 |
| 12.2.4 | A-12.2.4-TR95C | semantics | core | With tracing on, a select-line is reported once, with the line of the case whose case-list matches as the next line to be executed, and that case-line is reported once; the case-lines that do not match are not reported. | EXC-0134 |
| 12.2.5 | E-10007 | exception | core | Executing BREAK while debugging is active raises the nonfatal exception 10007; its recovery reports the BREAK line number and permits interaction with the debugging system. | EXC-0055, EXC-0056 |
| 12.2.5 | E-7401 | exception | core | Directing a trace report to an inactive channel raises the fatal exception 7401. | EXC-0057 |
| 12.2.5 | E-7402 | exception | core | Sending trace output to a channel whose file is not in display format and was not opened for OUTPUT or OUTIN access raises the fatal exception 7402. | EXC-0058, EXC-0059 |
| 13.1.3, 13.2.3 | A-ECMA-42 | syntax | graphics | The bare ECMA keyword forms WINDOW, VIEWPORT, CLIP, LINE STYLE and TEXT COLOR (without SET) are rejected by this ANSI interpreter (known deviation). | ECMA-0125 |
| 13.1.3 | A-13.1.3-EX | syntax | graphics | Every example of section 13.1.3 (set and ask of window, viewport, device window, device viewport, device size and clip) is accepted and behaves as written. | GFX-0014 |
| 13.1.3 | A-ECMA-37 | semantics | graphics | Window, viewport, device window, device viewport and clip settings (SET forms) and the corresponding ASK inquiries return the values set. | ECMA-0095, ECMA-0096 |
| 13.1.4 | A-13.1.4-01 | semantics | graphics | ASK WINDOW, ASK VIEWPORT, ASK DEVICE WINDOW and ASK DEVICE VIEWPORT give the left, right, bottom and top values, in that order, to the variables of the list, whether or not each of those variables was used earlier in the program. | GFX-0011, GFX-0012 |
| 13.1.4 | A-13.1.4-02 | semantics | graphics | ASK DEVICE SIZE gives the horizontal and vertical sizes to its first two numeric variables and the unit text to its string variable, whether or not those variables were used earlier in the program. | GFX-0013 |
| 13.1.4 | A-13.1.4-03 | semantics | graphics | SET WINDOW sets the window edges: the four parameters give the edges in problem coordinates, left first, then right, then bottom, then top, and the window starts as (0,1,0,1). | GFX-0019 |
| 13.1.4 | A-13.1.4-04 | semantics | graphics | SET VIEWPORT sets the viewport edges in normalized device coordinates, left, right, bottom, top in that order; each lies in [0,1] with left below right and bottom below top, and the viewport starts as (0,1,0,1). | GFX-0020 |
| 13.1.4 | A-13.1.4-05 | semantics | graphics | SET CLIP turns clipping to the viewport boundary on or off according to whether the string is ON or OFF in any letter case; clipping starts enabled. | GFX-0021 |
| 13.1.4 | A-13.1.4-07 | semantics | graphics | SET DEVICE WINDOW sets the device window edges in normalized device coordinates, left, right, bottom, top, each within [0,1] with left below right and bottom below top, starting as (0,1,0,1); output outside it is always clipped and the display is cleared when it is not already clear. | GFX-0022, GFX-0280, GFX-0281 |
| 13.1.4 | A-13.1.4-08 | semantics | graphics | SET DEVICE VIEWPORT sets the device viewport rectangle, in meters on devices with exactly scaled output and in device-dependent units otherwise, with the left and bottom edges of the surface at zero; it starts as the whole screen and clears the display when needed. | GFX-0024, GFX-0280, GFX-0281 |
| 13.1.4 | A-13.1.4-09 | semantics | graphics | An ask-statement with a status-clause stores zero in the status variable when the ask-object got meaningful values, otherwise the nonzero value defined for that ask-object; ask-objects that always succeed always store zero. | GFX-0025 |
| 13.1.4 | A-13.1.4-10 | semantics | graphics | ASK DEVICE SIZE stores the horizontal then vertical size of the available display surface in its two numeric variables and stores METERS or OTHER, in upper case, in its string variable. | GFX-0026 |
| 13.1.4 | A-13.1.4-11 | semantics | graphics | ASK CLIP stores ON or OFF, in upper case, in its string variable according to the current clipping state. | GFX-0027 |
| 13.1.4 | A-13.1.4-12 | semantics | graphics | ASK WINDOW returns the values established by the last SET WINDOW, in the order left, right, bottom, top. | GFX-0143 |
| 13.1.4 | A-13.1.4-13 | semantics | graphics | ASK CLIP stores ON or OFF, in upper case, according to the clipping state established by the last executed SET CLIP; every host stores it, including the command-line interpreter without --draw-log. | GFX-0156 |
| 13.1.5 | E-11051 | exception | graphics | Set-statement boundaries giving a rectangle of zero or negative width or height raise the nonfatal exception 11051 and keep the current values. | GFX-0103 |
| 13.1.5 | E-11052 | exception | graphics | A viewport boundary outside [0,1] raises the nonfatal exception 11052 and keeps the current viewport. | GFX-0104 |
| 13.1.5 | E-11053 | exception | graphics | A device window boundary outside [0,1] raises the nonfatal exception 11053 and keeps the current device window. | GFX-0105 |
| 13.1.5 | E-11054 | exception | graphics | A device viewport boundary outside the display space raises the nonfatal exception 11054 and keeps the current device viewport. | GFX-0106 |
| 13.1.5 | E-4101 | exception | graphics | A SET CLIP whose string is neither ON nor OFF after upper-casing raises the nonfatal exception 4101 and keeps the current clipping value. | GFX-0093 |
| 13.1.6 | A-13.1.6-01 | semantics | graphics | When an ask-object cannot return meaningful values, its status-clause receives 11000 plus the GKS error-indicator parameter value. | GFX-0028 |
| 13.2.3 | A-13.2.3-EX | syntax | graphics | Every example of section 13.2.3 (the set and ask objects for styles, colors, color mix and text) is accepted and behaves as written. | GFX-0015 |
| 13.2.3 | A-ECMA-38 | semantics | graphics | Line style and text color can be set and drawn with, and ASK MAX COLOR and ASK MAX POINT STYLE report the device limits. | ECMA-0097, ECMA-0098 |
| 13.2.4 | A-13.2.4-01 | semantics | graphics | CLEAR resets the graphic display when it is not already clear: erasing the screen on soft-copy devices and advancing the medium on hard-copy ones. | GFX-0029, GFX-0289 |
| 13.2.4 | A-13.2.4-02 | semantics | graphics | SET LINE STYLE or SET POINT STYLE rounds the index to an integer N and makes the Nth of the available styles current for later lines or points. | GFX-0030 |
| 13.2.4 | A-13.2.4-03 | semantics | graphics | At least four line styles exist: 1 solid, 2 dashed, 3 dotted, 4 dashed-dotted; the line style starts as one. | GFX-0031 |
| 13.2.4 | A-13.2.4-04 | semantics | graphics | At least five point styles exist: 1 dot, 2 plus, 3 asterisk, 4 circle, 5 x; the point style starts as three. | GFX-0032 |
| 13.2.4 | A-13.2.4-05 | semantics | graphics | ASK LINE STYLE or ASK POINT STYLE stores the number of the current line or point style. | GFX-0033 |
| 13.2.4 | A-13.2.4-06 | semantics | graphics | ASK MAX LINE STYLE or ASK MAX POINT STYLE stores the largest line or point style value available. | GFX-0034 |
| 13.2.4 | A-13.2.4-07 | semantics | graphics | Every style value from one up to the matching ASK MAX result is valid. | GFX-0035 |
| 13.2.4 | A-13.2.4-08 | semantics | graphics | SET POINT, LINE, TEXT or AREA COLOR rounds the index to an integer N and makes the Nth color the foreground for later points, lines, text or filled areas; all foreground indices start as one. | GFX-0036 |
| 13.2.4 | A-13.2.4-09 | semantics | graphics | ASK POINT, LINE, TEXT or AREA COLOR stores the current color index of that primitive. | GFX-0037 |
| 13.2.4 | A-13.2.4-10 | semantics | graphics | SET COLOR MIX rounds the index and sets the red, green and blue intensities of that index, each within [0,1]; index zero is the background color where meaningful. | GFX-0038 |
| 13.2.4 | A-13.2.4-11 | semantics | graphics | ASK COLOR MIX rounds the index and stores the red, green and blue intensities last set for it, or those actually in force; with a status-clause it stores 11086 for an out-of-range index and 11087 when no mix was set, returning zero intensities in both cases. | GFX-0039 |
| 13.2.4 | A-13.2.4-12 | semantics | graphics | ASK MAX COLOR stores the largest distinct color index usable by the color set-statements; every index from zero to it should be valid. | GFX-0040 |
| 13.2.4 | A-13.2.4-13 | semantics | graphics | ASK POINT, LINE, TEXT or AREA COLOR stores the color index established by the last SET for that primitive (the index rounded to an integer); every host stores it, including the command-line interpreter without --draw-log. | GFX-0157 |
| 13.2.4 | A-13.2.4-14 | semantics | graphics | ASK COLOR MIX stores the red, green and blue intensities established by the last executed SET COLOR MIX with the same index; every host stores them, including the command-line interpreter without --draw-log. | GFX-0158 |
| 13.2.5 | E-11056 | exception | graphics | A point style of zero or less, or above the available maximum, raises the nonfatal exception 11056 and uses style three. | GFX-0107 |
| 13.2.5 | E-11062 | exception | graphics | A line style of zero or less, or above the available maximum, raises the nonfatal exception 11062 and uses style one. | GFX-0108 |
| 13.2.5 | E-11073 | exception | graphics | A text height of zero or less raises the nonfatal exception 11073 and keeps the current height. | GFX-0109 |
| 13.2.5 | E-11085 | exception | graphics | A color index below zero or above the implementation maximum in a color set-statement or array-cells-statement raises the nonfatal exception 11085 and uses the implementation default. | GFX-0110, GFX-0137 |
| 13.2.5 | E-11088 | exception | graphics | A COLOR MIX component below zero or above one raises the nonfatal exception 11088 and keeps the current values. | GFX-0111 |
| 13.2.5 | E-4102 | exception | graphics | A SET TEXT JUSTIFY string outside the listed values raises the nonfatal exception 4102 and keeps the current justification. | GFX-0094 |
| 13.3.2 | A-13.3.2-01 | syntax | graphics | In an array-point-list two arrays must both be one-dimensional and a lone array two-dimensional; GRAPH LINES needs at least two coordinate-pairs and GRAPH AREA at least three. | GFX-0047, GFX-0048 |
| 13.3.2 | A-13.3.2-02 | syntax | graphics | The numeric-array of an array-cells-statement must be two-dimensional. | GFX-0049 |
| 13.3.2 | A-13.3.2-03 | syntax | graphics | GRAPH LINES must list at least two coordinate-pairs and GRAPH AREA at least three; a program that violates this is reported at load (STD 2.3 l.580-584), even when the statement sits in a branch that is never executed. | GFX-0152 |
| 13.3.2 | A-13.3.2-TR89 | syntax | graphics | When the dimensionality of the arrays is known at load, an array-point-list with two arrays whose arrays are not both one-dimensional, or with a lone array that is not two-dimensional (MAT GRAPH and MAT PLOT alike), and an array-cells-statement whose array is not two-dimensional, are rejected before the program runs; a lone two-dimensional array whose second dimension is not 2 is still the run-time exception 6401 (13.3.5). | GFX-0175, GFX-0176, GFX-0178 |
| 13.3.2 | A-13.3.2-TR94 | syntax | graphics | The dimensionality rule of an array-point-list also holds for MAT PLOT inside an internal picture whose arrays are declared by the containing program: it is rejected before the program runs. | GFX-0183, GFX-0184 |

| 15.1.4 | A-15.1.4-01 | semantics | fixed | When ARITHMETIC FIXED is selected, the values of numeric constants, variables and expressions behave as fixed-point decimal numbers; a variable can hold exactly the values expressible with its integer-size digits left of the point and fraction-size digits right of it, plus the sign, and the sign does not count toward the size. | FIX-0007 |
| 15.1.4 | A-15.1.4-02 | semantics | fixed | Numeric constants keep the semantics of section 5.1 except that each constant carries a precision attribute equal to its number of significant digits, and a constant written in scaled notation is read as the equivalent unscaled one. | FIX-0009 |
| 15.1.4 | A-15.1.4-03 | semantics | fixed | A numeric constant carrying more significant digits than P is rounded to no fewer than P digits; if the digits left of the point alone exceed P, an overflow exception results. | FIX-0011 |
| 15.1.4 | A-15.1.4-04 | semantics | fixed | A numeric expression used as a print item is always printed in unsealed representation: implicit point when no significant digit lies right of the point, explicit point otherwise, showing exactly the significant digits. | FIX-0014, FIX-0015 |
| 15.1.4 | A-15.1.4-05 | semantics | fixed | In NATIVE records, moving a value into an E-sized floating-point field preserves at least its first P significant digits exactly, and reading such a field back into a variable treats the field as a scaled numeric constant. | FIX-0017 |
| 15.1.4 | A-15.1.4-06 | semantics | fixed | For numeric data in a STREAM INTERNAL file written under the FIXED option, the DATUM ask-attribute reports the next datum's type as NUMERIC*!!.ff, with the two-digit integer-size and fraction-size of the datum as written (self-typed, l.12264-12267): a variable declared DECLARE NUMERIC*3.1 keeps 03.01 even under OPTION FIXED*8.2, and after a partial READ of a multi-datum WRITE the pending datum's own size is reported (§11.4.4 l.8056-8062). | FIX-0019 |
| 15.1.4 | A-15.1.4-07 | semantics | fixed | A numeric-variable under ARITHMETIC FIXED carries the significant digits it would have if spelled out as a constant with its full integer-size and fraction-size precision, and a print-item shows exactly those digits: a zero value prints with explicit point and all fraction-size digits (" .00 " in *5.2, " .0000 " in *8.4, also for values that round to zero such as .001), while with fraction-size 0 it prints with implicit point (" 0 " in *3.0); STR$ of the same value returns the print numeric-representation without the leading and trailing spaces (".00"). | FIX-0047, FIX-0048, FIX-0049 |
| 15.1.4 | A-15.1.4-08 | semantics | fixed | A numeric constant overflows only if the digits left of its point exceed P; with P of at least 18, a constant of 17 or 18 integer digits is valid under an ARITHMETIC FIXED option whose default size is smaller (for example *4.2): a print-item prints it with exactly its digits, it can be assigned to a variable whose integer-size holds it, and assigning it to a variable whose integer-size does not hold it raises 1011 and leaves the variable unchanged. | FIX-0050 |
| 15.1.4 | A-15.1.4-109 | semantics | fixed | Reading a wide FIXED variable (for example *18.0 holding 17 or 18 integer digits) in a comparison or in an arithmetic expression under an ARITHMETIC FIXED option with a smaller default size never raises 1011, which is the exception of assigning to a variable; a comparison cannot overflow, and the result of an expression overflows (1002, numeric-expression overflow) only when its integer digits do not fit in P. The precision of the result of an expression is implementation-defined; this implementation keeps up to P+2 significant digits and, when the integer digits need the room, reduces the fraction digits (rounding) down to zero, so 12345678901234567 + 1 is exact. | FIX-0151 |
| 15.1.4 | A-15.1.4-110 | semantics | fixed | Assigning a numeric value to a fixed-point variable or array element, by LET or from READ or INPUT, rounds the digits beyond the fraction-size of the receiving variable (the rounding rule is implementation-defined, half away from zero here, D-15.1-7); the operands of the expression assigned keep their own precision until that moment, so 1.555 = 1.56 is false while LET B = 1.555 stores 1.56, and a FOR loop with a step finer than the control variable rounds the control variable at every step. | FIX-0174 |
| 15.1.4 | A-15.1.4-FI14 | semantics | fixed | Under ARITHMETIC FIXED a numeric-constant keeps its own precision (the significant digits written) when it is written to an INTERNAL file: reading it back gives the same value as assigning the constant, and DATUM reports its own integer-size and fraction-size (0.12345 is NUMERIC*00.05 even under FIXED*8.2). | FIX-0179 |
| 15.1.5 | E-1001 | exception | fixed | A numeric constant whose integer-part significant digits exceed the maximum precision P raises fatal exception 1001, an overflow while evaluating a numeric constant. | FIX-0020 |

| 15.1.5 | E-1011 | exception | fixed | Assigning a numeric value to a fixed-decimal variable, fixed parameter or fixed defined function when the value's integer part needs more digits than the target's integer-size raises fatal exception 1011, an overflow in a fixed decimal assignment. | FIX-0024 |
| 15.2.2 | A-15.2.2-01 | syntax | fixed | A numeric variable or actual array passed in a CALL must match the procedure parameter in both integer-size and fraction-size; for other numeric arguments only the ARITHMETIC options of the two program units must agree. | FIX-0025, FIX-0026 |
| 15.2.2 | A-15.2.2-02 | syntax | fixed | The OPTION ARITHMETIC FIXED statement must be on a lower-numbered line than any internal function definition that declares a numeric defined function or has numeric parameters. | FIX-0027 |
| 15.2.2 | A-15.2.2-03 | syntax | fixed | A fixed-point-type on an internal function line or DEF statement, and a numeric-fixed-parameter, may be used only when the program unit has selected ARITHMETIC FIXED. | FIX-0028, FIX-0029 |
| 15.2.2 | A-15.2.2-04 | syntax | fixed | If a function type declares a fixed defined function, the fixed-point sizes stated, whether explicit or by default, in the declaration and in the matching definition must agree. | FIX-0030 |
| 15.2.3 | A-15.2.3-EX | syntax | fixed | Every parameter and function form shown in the examples of section 15.2.3, fixed formal arrays, fixed defined functions and external functions, is accepted and behaves as written. | FIX-0031 |
| 15.2.3 | A-ECMA-41 | syntax | fixed | Fixed-decimal sizes on arrays and function signatures (A()*8.2, DEF F*10.3(...)) are rejected at load time (known deviation). | ECMA-0103, ECMA-0104 |
| 15.2.4 | A-15.2.4-01 | semantics | fixed | Under ARITHMETIC FIXED, numeric procedure parameters, function parameters and defined functions hold fixed-point decimal values; one whose fixed-point-size is not written takes the default of the ARITHMETIC FIXED option, and a formal array's size applies to each element. | FIX-0032 |
| 15.2.4 | A-15.2.4-02 | semantics | fixed | Arguments of a function reference are bound to the function parameters as in 9.1, except that when the argument's fixed-point-size differs from the parameter's the fixed-point assignment rules of 15.1.4 are used. | FIX-0033 |
| 15.2.4 | A-15.2.4-03 | semantics | fixed | Arguments of a CALL are associated with the subprogram parameters as in 9.2, except that a numeric-expression argument, other than a plain variable, whose fixed-point-size differs from the parameter's is converted using the 15.1.4 assignment rules. | FIX-0034 |

### Agreed interpretations

Readings adopted by this implementation where the standard admits more than one reading or leaves the choice to the project:

| ECMA clause | Topic | Reading adopted | Standard lines |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7.3.5 | String overflow when a string-array expression is assigned to an array with a smaller length-max | The overflow of the length-max of the receiving array is reported as 1106, raised by the assignment (l.3468). 1052 (l.3465) is raised by evaluating the expression when an element of the result would exceed the maximum string length of the implementation, 1E9 characters (D-6.2-2): the MAT concatenation raises it before building the element. | l.3465, l.3468 |
| 9.2.2 | DECLARE INTERNAL SUB in the example of 9.2.6 | Rejected as a syntax error: the syntax of 9.2.2 is internal-sub-type = SUB sub-list, and ECMA-116 has the same production, so the word INTERNAL in the example of 9.2.6 (100 DECLARE INTERNAL SUB S) is an erratum of the example; DECLARE SUB S runs it as written. | l.4497-4499, l.4819 |
| 12.1.4 | Leaving an exception-handler by EXIT FOR or EXIT DO | An EXIT FOR or EXIT DO in a handler, for a loop that contains the whole when-block, is accepted and leaves the handler with no further effect, as an end-when-line does. The four means of exiting listed in 12.1.4 describe the handler-return statements and are not stated as a restriction. | l.8818-8840 |
| 15.2.2 | ARITHMETIC agreement between program-units joined by CHAIN, and the ordering rule of OPTION ARITHMETIC FIXED | 15.2.2 l.12354-12357 requires only that the ARITHMETIC options of the two program-units agree in type (both DECIMAL, both NATIVE or both FIXED), not in fixed-point precision: CHAIN from FIXED*4.2 to FIXED*8.2 runs without 4303, while NATIVE vs DECIMAL raises 4303 both ways. The ordering rule of 15.1.2 l.12145-12148 applies to numeric expressions, variables and NUMERIC declare-statements of the program-unit, not to the numeric parameters of the program-name-line (the first line), so a FIXED program with numeric program parameters is conforming. | l.12354-12357, l.12145-12148 |

## 5. Implementation-defined values

Appendix C of the standard lists the features whose value each implementation chooses; the claimed items and their values are:

| ECMA clause | Claim ID | Module | Item | Value | Tests |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.3 | D-2.3-1 | core | How syntactically illegal constructs are interpreted, a point Appendix C subsection 2.3 leaves to each implementation. | They are rejected at load time: the program is never executed, every syntax error found is listed on stderr and the CLI exits with status 1 (measured: '10 PARALLEL' is rejected with a load-time syntax error because the real-time module is not implemented). | PRG-0013 |
| 2.3 | D-2.3-2 | core | Format of error messages, a point Appendix C subsection 2.3 leaves to each implementation. | Load-time errors are reported on stderr as the header 'Error loading the program:' followed by one line per error '  ERROR <code>: line N[:C] - <msg>' (syntax errors carry the code E-SYNTAX, e.g. '  ERROR E-SYNTAX: line 20:7 - Syntax error: ...') plus the closing line '  Error processing the source code'; exit status 1. Load-time warnings (the 1010 of a fixed-point-size above P) go to stderr under 'Warnings while loading the program:' as '  WARNING <code>: line N:C - <msg>' and the program runs. The messages are in English. Measured with the CLI (the FBCS harness only asserts the rejection, not the text). | PRG-0013 |
| 2.4 | D-2.4-1 | core | Format of exception messages, a point Appendix C subsection 2.4 leaves to each implementation (the report must at least identify the code and the line, l.619-621). | An uncaught nonfatal exception prints on STDOUT 'Warning <code>: line N:C - <msg> (<clause>)' and execution continues (exit 0), e.g. 'Warning 3101: line 20:10 - Uninitialized numeric-variable 'X' (5.2)'; measured with the CLI: stderr stays empty, and if a PRINT with a pending end-of-line was in progress the warning is interleaved into that output line. An uncaught fatal exception prints 'ERROR <code>: line N[:C] - <msg>' on stderr and terminates the program (exit 1), e.g. 'ERROR 3001: line 20:10 - Division by zero'; load-time errors also go to stderr (D-2.3-2). All the texts of the CLI are in English since 2026-11-11. Measured with the CLI. A nonfatal exception raised in the middle of a PRINT (TAB, USING$, an uninitialized variable) prints its report at once, before the rest of the line, as the NBS test P008 requires (an X in column 1 after the system message); only the 8203 of a PRINT USING without a final separator is reported after the end-of-line of the statement. | PRT-0001, PRT-0157 |
| 2.4 | D-2.4-2 | core | Hardware-dependent exceptions and how resource-constraint exceptions out of the standard's fixed recovery are handled, a point Appendix C subsection 2.4 leaves to each implementation. | No hardware-dependent exceptions beyond the standard's are defined. Underflow policy (1500 series, all nonfatal, value 0 supplied): 1502, 1503, 1504, 1506 and 1507 are raised and, uncaught, print a Warning line (measured: LET A = 1E-300*1E-300 -> Warning 1502; EXP(-800) -> Warning 1503; VAL('1E-400') -> Warning 1504; DATA 1E-400 -> Warning 1506; INPUT of 1E-400 -> Warning 1507); 1501 is catchable in a WHEN block (EXTYPE 1501, NUM-0006) but prints no uncaught Warning (LET X = 1E-401 yields 0 silently); 1505 and 1508 are never raised (E-1505/E-1508 not-applicable). Overflow raises fatal 1002/1003 in expressions and functions. The depth of procedure invocation (CALL, function invocation and GOSUB together) is limited to 100000 levels: the invocation that would exceed it raises the fatal implementation exception -10011 before entering, catchable in a when-block (EXTYPE -110011 when propagated out of the procedure, 12.1.4 l.8909-8913; EXC-0264). | NUM-0006, NUM-0032, NUM-0058, STR-0040, PRT-0025, PRT-0047, EXC-0264 |
| 2.4 | D-2.4-3 | core | Order of exception detection in a line, a point Appendix C subsection 2.4 leaves to each implementation. | When a single statement raises several exceptions, the first one in evaluation order is detected and reported; operands are evaluated right-to-left (D-5.3-1), so in 'PRINT SQR(-1) + 1/0' the division by zero (3001) is reported and in 'PRINT 1/0 + SQR(-1)' the square root of a negative (3005) is reported. Measured with the CLI. | NUM-0033 |
| 3.2 | D-3.2-1 | core | The semantic rules for native data (collating sequence, precision) that the definition of 'native' in subsection 3.2 leaves implementation-defined (Appendix C, subsection 3.2). | Native data follows the host model: strings are sequences of Latin-1 characters, one position each (LEN of 'ñ' is 1, D-4.1-1), the native collating sequence is character-code order identical to STANDARD (D-4.1.4-1, D-6.6-1), CHR$/ORD use character codes 0..255 (D-6.4-1, D-6.4-2), and NATIVE arithmetic is backed by binary64 and quantized to 8 significant digits (D-5.6-3: fpScale 8; measured NUM-0243: 1/3*3 - 1 = -1E-8 and 1/3 - .33333333 = 0), which exceeds the 6 significant digits the standard requires (NUM-0082: 1/3 within 5E-7, MAXNUM > 1E+38, EPS(0) < 2E-38); values are printed with d = 8 digits under NATIVE as under DECIMAL (D-10.3-2). | PRG-0023, STR-0059, NUM-0082, NUM-0243 |
| 4.1.4 | D-4.1.4-1 | core | Coding used for the native collating sequence under OPTION COLLATE NATIVE, which Appendix C leaves to each implementation. | OPTION COLLATE NATIVE orders strings by character code (ASCII, then the Latin-1 other-characters 128..255), identical to STANDARD for all input; no locale-aware collation is implemented. | PRG-0023 |
| 4.1.6 | D-4.1-1 | core | Meaning of other-characters beyond ASCII: what they do in strings, in input data, in files and in CHR$ values, which Appendix C leaves to each implementation. | Other-characters are the Latin-1 (ISO/IEC 8859-1) characters at ordinal positions 128..255, one position per character: LEN, substrings and MAXLEN count characters (the e-acute has LEN 1), and they are accepted inside quoted strings, in unquoted data (INPUT, DATA, DISPLAY files) at any position, and in remarks. The program text is UTF-8 and is converted to Latin-1 on loading; a character outside Latin-1 (U+0100 and above) anywhere in the source, comments included, is a load error (E-NOT-LATIN1, with line and column), and one in input data or in a DISPLAY file is exception 8102 (INPUT, LINE INPUT, MAT INPUT) or 8105 (file); console and graphic text leave as UTF-8; DISPLAY files (sequential, stream, relative and keyed, keys included) are stored in UTF-8 on disk with RECSIZE and MARGIN counted in characters, while INTERNAL and NATIVE files keep the Latin-1 bytes unconverted. CHR$(n) yields the character at position n for 0..255 (ORD(CHR$(233)) = 233 and ORD("é") = 233); ORD rejects a string of more than one character with exception 4003. UCASE$ and LCASE$ convert every Latin-1 letter (sharp s and y-diaeresis have no one-character counterpart and stay), and strings compare by character code ("z" < "ñ"). The standard character set has 256 characters: the 128 ASCII characters plus 128 additional other-characters in ordinal positions 128..255 (Tabla 8 l.12768-12770 leaves the number implementation-defined; here 128), so CHR$(127.5) rounds to 128 and is legal (no 4002). | PRG-0025, PRG-0026, PRG-0080, PRG-0081, STR-0093, STR-0094 |
| 4.2.2 | D-4.2-1 | core | How the end of a line is recognised (carriage return, return plus line feed, end of record, ...), which Appendix C leaves to each implementation. | End-of-line is LF (0x0A); a CRLF pair is also accepted (the CR is discarded); a lone CR is not an end-of-line (lexer error). PRG-0034 reads its own source back line by line. | PRG-0034 |
| 4.2.2 | D-4.2-2 | core | Actual maximum physical line length accepted, which Appendix C lists as implementation-defined even though 132 characters is the limit the standard states. | The maximum physical line length accepted is exactly 132 characters (STD §4.2.2 l.1329): a 132-character line is accepted (PRG-0035) and a 133-character line is rejected at load with E-LINE-TOO-LONG (PRG-0033). | PRG-0035 |
| 4.2.4 | D-4.2-4 | core | How the program designator of a CHAIN relates to the program name, which Appendix C leaves to each implementation. | The CHAIN designator is a file path only; the PROGRAM name of the target is not compared with the designator (measured: CHAIN "tgt" ran tgt.BAS declaring PROGRAM OtherName). A missing file raises fatal exception 10005, which PRG-0036 verifies via WHEN/USE and EXTYPE. | PRG-0036 |
| 4.4.6 | D-4.4-1 | core | Extra limits an operating system may put on the length and form of identifiers of procedures compiled separately from the main program, which Appendix C leaves to each implementation. | No separate compilation exists (all procedures live in one source file), so the OS imposes no extra limits on procedure identifiers; external-sub names of 31 characters (and longer) are accepted. | PRG-0059 |
| 5.1 | D-5.1-1 | core | The precision and the range kept for numeric constants (Appendix C, subsection 5.1) are chosen by the implementation, within the minimums fixed by section 5.1.4. | Numeric constants are held as exact decimals up to 18 significant digits (printed with 8 significant digits (d = 8, D-10.3-2) under DECIMAL and NATIVE alike); magnitude range EPS(0)=2.2250738585073E-308 to MAXNUM=1.7976931348623157E+308 under DECIMAL (D-5.4-2). | NUM-0007 |
| 5.2 | D-5.2-1 | core | The value every numeric variable holds when execution starts (Appendix C, subsection 5.2) is chosen by the implementation. | Every numeric variable starts at 0; a read before any assignment also raises the nonfatal exception 3101 (EXTYPE 3101) and supplies 0. The same holds for an array element read by MAT PRINT, MAT PRINT USING, MAT WRITE or MAT GRAPH: the statement supplies 0, completes, and raises 3101 once (3102 for a string array). | NUM-0014, ARR-0210, ARR-0211, ARR-0212, ARR-0213, ARR-0214 |
| 5.3 | D-5.3-1 | core | Beyond the fixed precedence and left-to-right grouping rules, the order in which the parts of a numeric expression are evaluated (Appendix C, subsection 5.3) is chosen by the implementation. | Operands of an operator are evaluated right-to-left in source order (with a side-effecting internal FUNCTION INC, INC(0)*10+INC(0) yields 21, i.e. the right call is evaluated first); grouping itself stays left-to-right per 5.3.4. | NUM-0033 |
| 5.4 | D-5.4-1 | core | The accuracy with which built-in numeric functions are evaluated (Appendix C, subsection 5.4) is chosen by the implementation. | Under DECIMAL every numeric function (SQR, EXP, LOG, LOG10, LOG2, SIN, COS, TAN, SEC, CSC, COT, ATN, ANGLE, ASIN, ACOS, SINH, COSH, TANH) and the power operator are computed in decimal with 34 working digits and rounded once to the 18-digit result, so each is the true value rounded to 18 digits (error at most 5 units in the 19th digit, the 5.6.4 bound for m = 17; measured on 2026-11-08); under NATIVE they are computed in binary64 and quantized to 8 significant digits; values print with 8 significant digits (d = 8, D-10.3-2). | NUM-0059 |
| 5.4 | D-5.4-2 | core | The values of MAXNUM and of EPS (Appendix C, subsection 5.4) are chosen by the implementation. | MAXNUM = 1.7976931348623157E+308 and EPS(0) = sigma = 2.2250738585073E-308 under DECIMAL (the IEEE-754 binary64 limits; DBL_MIN kept with 14 digits); under NATIVE MAXNUM = 1.7976931E+308 and EPS(0) = 2.2250739E-308 (DBL_MAX and DBL_MIN quantized to 8 digits); under FIXED *i.f, MAXNUM is the largest value of P digits and EPS(0) = 10^-f (.001 under *8.3), the smallest positive value representable in the mode. | NUM-0060 |
| 5.4 | D-5.4-3 | core | The pseudorandom sequence from which RND draws its values (Appendix C, subsection 5.4) is chosen by the implementation. | RND draws from the C library rand() sequence seeded with 1 when RANDOMIZE is not executed (first values .417022, .99718481, .72032449, .93255736, 1.1438108E-4, printed to d = 8 digits, D-10.3-2); RANDOMIZE reseeds from the system clock. | NUM-0061 |
| 5.4 | D-5.4-4 | core | Whether a calendar and a clock are available to DATE and TIME (Appendix C, subsection 5.4) is chosen by the implementation. | A calendar and a clock are available: DATE returns the YYDDD of the local date (26305 on 2026-11-01) and TIME returns seconds since local midnight (0 <= TIME < 86400); neither yields -1 on this host. | NUM-0062 |
| 5.4 | D-5.4-5 | core | The time zone used by DATE and TIME (Appendix C, subsection 5.4) is chosen by the implementation. | The host local time zone (Europe/Madrid: CET UTC+1 in winter, CEST UTC+2 in summer) is used for DATE and TIME. | NUM-0063 |
| 5.6 | D-5.6-1 | core | The precision and range of numeric values in general (Appendix C, subsection 5.6) are chosen by the implementation. | Default arithmetic is decimal floating point with a documented precision m = 17 significant digits (what the operations + - * / and the constants meet, error at most 5 units in the 19th digit); values are held with an 18-digit mantissa and EPS reflects that representation (EPS(1) = 1E-17); range EPS(0)=2.2250738585073E-308 .. MAXNUM=1.7976931348623157E+308, printed with 8 significant digits (d = 8, D-10.3-2). The supplied functions and the power operator meet this precision too (A-5.6.4-FN1). | NUM-0080 |
| 5.6 | D-5.6-2 | core | The precision and range of the decimal floating-point arithmetic (Appendix C, subsection 5.6) are chosen by the implementation. | OPTION ARITHMETIC DECIMAL: exact decimal floating point, documented precision m = 17, 18-digit mantissa in variables and intermediates (EPS(1) = 1E-17), range 2.2250738585073E-308 .. 1.7976931348623157E+308; 0.1+0.2 = 0.3 exactly. | NUM-0081 |
| 5.6 | D-5.6-3 | core | The precision and range of native arithmetic (Appendix C, subsection 5.6) are chosen by the implementation. | OPTION ARITHMETIC NATIVE: same binary64-backed values quantized to 8 significant digits (fpScale 8); range 2.2250739E-308 .. 1.7976931E+308; observed precision 8 digits (at least 6 required). | NUM-0082, NUM-0243 |
| 5.6 | D-5.6-4 | core | The accuracy of numeric expression evaluation (Appendix C, subsection 5.6) is chosen by the implementation. | With m = 17: constants, the operations + - * / and every numeric function and power err at most 5 units in the 19th significant digit and are exact when the true result fits in 18 digits (0.1+0.2 = 0.3). The transcendental functions are computed in decimal with 34 working digits and rounded once to 18 digits; the measurement of 2026-11-08 gives m = 17 for all of them, in radians and degrees, including the ill-conditioned zones. | NUM-0083, NUM-0281 |
| 6.2 | D-6.2-1 | core | Value held by every string variable when execution begins, before any assignment. | Null string: reading a string variable before assignment raises nonfatal 3102 (catchable); uncaught, a warning is issued and the value used is the null string (LEN 0). | STR-0013 |
| 6.2 | D-6.2-2 | core | Default maximum length of a string variable that has no declared length limit (the default string length limit, at least 132). | The effective limit of 1E9 characters (one limit for every string): MAXLEN of an undeclared string variable returns 1000000000, above the required minimum of 132. A string expression whose result would be longer raises the fatal 1051 (REPEAT$, concatenation, substring assignment; E-1051) and a string-array expression the fatal 1052 (MAT concatenation, 7.3.5; E-1052); the length is checked before the string is built. | STR-0014, STR-0091 |
| 6.4 | D-6.4-1 | core | CHR$ results for the native character set. | CHR$(M) returns the character with code M of the Latin-1 set (CHR$(65)="A", CHR$(48)="0", CHR$(233)="é"); under COLLATE NATIVE the native set applies. | STR-0056 |
| 6.4 | D-6.4-2 | core | ORD results for the native character set. | ORD under the native set returns the character code (ASCII, or Latin-1 for 128..255): ORD("A")=65, ORD("a")=97, ORD("5")=53, ORD(" ")=32, ORD("é")=233. | STR-0057 |
| 6.4 | D-6.4-3 | core | Whether a calendar and a clock are available to DATE$ and TIME$. | Calendar and clock are available: DATE$ returns the host date as YYYYMMDD and TIME$ the host time as HH:MM:SS; the no-device values "00000000" and "99:99:99" are unreachable here. | STR-0058 |
| 6.6 | D-6.6-1 | core | Collating sequence used under OPTION COLLATE NATIVE. | Ordering by character code (ASCII, then the Latin-1 other-characters 128..255), which coincides with Table 8 over the ASCII range 0..127. | STR-0059 |
| 6.6 | D-6.6-2 | core | Maximum length of a declared string variable that has no length-max (the implementation-defined default). | The effective limit of 1E9 characters: MAXLEN of a declared variable without length-max returns 1000000000, above the required 132. A length-max above that limit (DECLARE STRING A$*2000000000, also in a string-type, a string array, a DEF or a FUNCTION) is rejected at load with E-STRING-LENGTH-MAX-TOO-LARGE, because the length-max guarantees that values of that length can be stored (6.6.4 l.2886-2896; decision of the project owner, 2026-11-12; measured with the CLI). | STR-0060, STR-0095 |
| 7.1.4 | D-7.1-1 | core | Default maximum length of an element of a string array when neither the declaration nor the string type sets a length limit. | The effective limit of 1E9 characters: MAXLEN of a string array declared without length-max returns 1000000000 and strings of 200 characters are stored whole (far above the required minimum of 132). | ARR-0137 |
| 9.3.4 | D-9.3-1 | core | How a program designator in CHAIN is associated with a program. | The designator is a file name resolved against the current working directory of the interpreter process; the named file must contain the chained BASIC program. | SEG-0304 |
| 9.3.4 | D-9.3-2 | core | Whether upper-case and lower-case letters are equivalent in a program designator. | Case is not significant on this build's default macOS APFS volume (resolution follows the host file system): CHAIN 'mixedcase.bas' runs the file written as MixedCase.BAS. | SEG-0305 |
| 9.3.4 | D-9.3-3 | core | Initial values of the variables of a chained-to program. | Numeric variables start at 0 and string variables at empty (the uninitialized-variable policy, warnings 3101/3102); observed inside the chained-to program. | SEG-0306 |
| 9.3.6 | D-9.3-4 | core | Which program reports the exceptions 4301, 4302 and 4303 of a chain-statement, and whether the chained-from program's WHEN can intercept them. | The interpreter reports them itself (as the chained-from side) as FATAL exceptions localized at the CHAIN statement; they are NOT interceptable by a WHEN handler of the chained-from program. STD §9.3.6 l.4927-4932 allows the chained-from program, the chained-to program or an intermediate system program to report them, so no WHEN interception is promised; this implementation chooses the interpreter, fatal. | SEG-0307, SEG-0308, SEG-0310, SEG-0313 |
| 10.3.4 | D-10.3-1 | core | Effect when a function called during a PRINT prints to the same device (Appendix C, subsection 10.3 item 1). | The function's output goes to the same device in evaluation order, sharing the columnar position: PRINT "a"; F(1); "b" with a function that does PRINT "[in]"; writes a[in] 1 b on one line, and when the function ends its own line (PRINT "SIDE", PRT-0079) the outer PRINT continues on the next one. | PRT-0079 |
| 10.3.6 | D-10.3-7 | core | Whether the trailing space of a printed number is emitted when it would push the column past the margin (Appendix C, subsection 10.3 item 7). | The trailing space of a printed number is always emitted; when the whole number field would cross the margin, an end-of-line is generated first (l.5484), so the space is never dropped. | PRT-0085 |
| 10.3.6 | D-10.3-8 | core | Case of the E letter used in scaled numeric output (Appendix C, subsection 10.3 item 8). | The E of scaled numeric output is uppercase. | PRT-0086 |
| 11 | D-11-1 | files | The effect of file-organization and record-type combinations beyond those of the core and enhanced modules is implementation-defined. | Unlisted organization/record-type combinations are accepted and processed according to the record type. STREAM+DISPLAY: PRINT # writes one line per statement, as for SEQUENTIAL+DISPLAY (so PRINT #n: 1, 2, 3 writes ONE line with print zones, 10.3.4.3, and reading it back with READ #n: X into a numeric variable raises 8101, 11.4.5.3 l.8430-8431, because the zone-padded text is not a single numeric-constant), but reading follows the stream rule of 11.4.4.8 (l.8224-8235): INPUT #, READ # and MAT INPUT # take their data from the sequence of data in the file, line boundaries are not significant (a line with too few data does not raise 8012: the next line supplies the rest; only the end of the file raises 8011) and the data left over from the current line are the next file elements; LINE INPUT # and MAT LINE INPUT # return the unread rest of the current line as it is, spaces included, when data are pending, and the next line otherwise; MAT INPUT X(?) takes the pending data of the current line or, if none, the data of the next line that has any. STREAM+NATIVE needs a TEMPLATE like any NATIVE file and follows the same stream rule: there are no records, so READ # takes the next fields of the file whatever the previous statement read, a template longer than the data left raises 8011 at the end of the file, and 8012/8013 never occur. Files written by builds before 2026-11-09 are not read: no released version wrote them. | FIL-0152, FIL-0601 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-1 | files | The maximum channel number is implementation-defined (the standard only requires it to be at least 99). | 255 (channels 0..255; channel 256 raises 7001). | FIL-0153 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-10 | files | The length of records of type INTERNAL and NATIVE is implementation-defined. | INTERNAL records are stored as typed tag+payload values (tag u8: 0x01 double LE, 0x02 FIXED scaled, 0x03 string u32len+bytes, 0x04 exact DECIMAL); NATIVE records as fixed template fields; record length varies with the values. | FIL-0160 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-11 | files | When RECSIZE omits the LENGTH index, the maximum record length of the file is implementation-defined. | MAXNUM: no effective limit on record length (ASK RECSIZE reports VARIABLE). | FIL-0055 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-12 | files | The DATUM ask-value for file organizations other than STREAM INTERNAL is implementation-defined. | 'UNKNOWN' for a SEQUENTIAL DISPLAY file (null string on an inactive channel); DATUM is only well-defined for STREAM INTERNAL files. | FIL-0161 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-13 | files | The NAME ask-value returned for channel zero is implementation-defined. | The null string. | FIL-0162 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-14 | files | The meaning of the implementation-defined file-access failure codes 7101 through 7199 is implementation-defined. | 7107 = file does not exist; 7108 = invalid file name, raised by an OPEN whose NAME is the empty string (a name of spaces is not empty), for every ACCESS and ORGANIZATION (11.1.5 l.7069-7072). | FIL-0163, FIL-0564 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-15 | files | The maximum length of a key in a KEYED file is implementation-defined. | At least 10000 characters; no limit observed. | FIL-0164 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-2 | files | Whether file names differing only in letter case denote the same file or different files is implementation-defined. | Case-insensitive on the host filesystem: names differing only in letter case denote the same file. | FIL-0154 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-3 | files | Opening a file that is already open has implementation-defined consequences. | Opening an already-open file on another channel succeeds; both channels then share the file. | FIL-0155 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-4 | files | How many nonzero channels beyond the required minimum may be active simultaneously is implementation-defined. | At least 10 nonzero channels may be active simultaneously (observed 10 of 10). | FIL-0156 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-5 | files | Whether a file closed and later reopened with different organization, record type or record size remains accessible is implementation-defined. | The file remains accessible when reopened with a different organization or record type (observed RELATIVE and INTERNAL reopens of a SEQUENTIAL DISPLAY file). | FIL-0157 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-6 | files | For INTERNAL and NATIVE files, whether a reopen under a different ARITHMETIC option keeps the file accessible is implementation-defined. | An INTERNAL file reopened under OPTION ARITHMETIC NATIVE remains accessible with its contents preserved (observed 1.5 read back unchanged). | FIL-0158 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-7 | files | Accessing an INTERNAL or NATIVE file from another program unit under a different ARITHMETIC option has implementation-defined results. | Access under a different ARITHMETIC option works (observed reopen of an INTERNAL file under OPTION ARITHMETIC NATIVE, contents preserved). | FIL-0158 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-8 | files | The means a user employs to keep file contents unchanged between runs of a program is implementation-defined. | Ordinary files in the working directory persist between runs of the program; no special means is needed. | FIL-0159 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-9 | files | The effect of organization and record-type combinations not listed for any conforming module is implementation-defined. | Same as D-11-1: unlisted combinations are accepted and processed according to the record type. | FIL-0152 |
| 11.1.5 | A-11.1.5-02 | files | The 71xx exception for an OPEN whose access to the file is not possible is fatal when unhandled; the value of xx is implementation-defined (Table 9 l.12916-12917). | FullBASIC raises 7107 (file does not exist) for OPEN ... ACCESS INPUT of a nonexistent file; the example in 12.1 (l.8742-8744) uses 7107 for that case. | FIL-0019 |
| 11.2 | D-11.2-1 | files | What condition on a non-file device channel makes the data-found condition false is implementation-defined. | On channel zero (the only device) the data-found condition is true whenever input data is available and false when the standard input is at its end (D-11.2-2). | FIL-0165 |
| 11.2 | D-11.2-2 | files | Whether the end of the standard input is the implementation-defined condition of a device signifying that no data is available for input, so that the missing-recovery of INPUT #0 and LINE INPUT #0 takes effect, is implementation-defined. | It is: with the standard input at its end, INPUT #0 and LINE INPUT #0 take their IF MISSING recovery (a line number or EXIT DO); without IF MISSING they raise the fatal exception 8011. | FIL-0600 |
| 11.2 | D-11.2-3 | files | The largest record number of a RELATIVE file, and the exception raised when a larger one is requested, are implementation-defined. | Record numbers go from 1 to 4294967295 (the file format keeps them in 32 bits). A RECORD index above that, and a WRITE or PRINT without record-setter in the area after record 4294967295, raise the fatal exception 7206, the only code of the exception table for an invalid RECORD index, and change nothing in the file. | FIL-0602 |
| 11.3 | D-11.3-1 | files | The means by which the end of a stored file element is signalled is implementation-defined. | DISPLAY records are stored as newline-terminated lines. | FIL-0166 |
| 11.3 | D-11.3-2 | files | The default margin and the default zone width of a DISPLAY file are implementation-defined. | Default zone width 17 = d+e+6 (d = 8, e = 3; STD 11.3.4.4 l.7618-7621) for a DISPLAY file; margin unlimited for files (ASK #n: MARGIN reports MAXNUM, Table 5 l.6993-6995), 132 for channel zero. | FIL-0167 |
| 11.3 | D-11.3-3 | files | The largest margin and the largest zone width a file supports are implementation-defined. | At least 1000000 for both the margin and the zone width. | FIL-0168 |
| 11.3 | D-11.3-4 | files | The accuracy of numeric values printed into DISPLAY records is implementation-defined. | 8 significant digits (d = 8, D-10.3-2; 1/3 prints as .33333333, 123456789012345678 as 1.2345679E+17). | FIL-0169 |
| 11.4 | D-11.4-1 | files | How many significant digits a value received from a numeric field of a NATIVE record keeps is implementation-defined. | A NUMERIC*i.f field stores fixed-point decimal text of that size: 1/3 in NUMERIC*15.10 reads back as .3333333333 (lossy beyond the 10 fraction digits). | FIL-0170 |
| 11.4 | D-11.4-2 | files | The effect of the prompt, timeout and time-inquiry controls on true files and nonterminal devices is implementation-defined. | PROMPT, TIMEOUT and ELAPSED are accepted on true files and ignored (no prompt is shown, no timeout applies). | FIL-0171, FIL-0181 |
| 11.4 | D-11.4-3 | files | The precision of numeric constants received back from DISPLAY files is implementation-defined. | Numeric constants are retrieved with full numeric-constant accuracy (0.1 reads back exactly as 0.1). | FIL-0172 |
| 11.4 | D-11.4-4 | files | The precision with which numeric values can be retrieved without loss from a NATIVE file is implementation-defined. | Same storage as D-11.4-1: fixed-point decimal fields of the template size, exact only within those digits. | FIL-0170 |
| 11.4 | D-11.4-5 | files | Retrieving a NATIVE record whose contents are incompatible with the TEMPLATE used has implementation-defined results. | Reading a NATIVE record with an incompatible TEMPLATE raises 8012 (record too short for the TEMPLATE). | FIL-0173 |
| 11.4 | D-11.4-6 | files | Whether an illegal input reply on a device is treated with the fatal section 11 procedure or the nonfatal section 10 recovery is implementation-defined. | On channel zero an illegal input reply raises the nonfatal 8103 (section 10 device recovery), not the fatal 8105. | FIL-0174 |
| 11.5 | D-11.5-1 | files | The effect of REWRITE and DELETE on files whose organization is not RELATIVE or KEYED is implementation-defined. | REWRITE and DELETE on a SEQUENTIAL or STREAM file raise the local code -7500 (organization not supported), whatever the record type (DISPLAY, INTERNAL or NATIVE); the code is negative because the effect is outside the standard ranges. | FIL-0175, FIL-0567 |
| 11.5 | D-11.5-2 | files | Using an incompatible TEMPLATE that contains SKIP in a REWRITE has implementation-defined results. | REWRITE with a template without SKIP over a SKIP-created NATIVE record succeeds and replaces the record. | FIL-0176 |
| 12.1 | D-12.1-1 | core | Which EXTYPE value a local enhancement assigns to each of its own exceptions (Appendix C, subsection 12.1 item 1). | Negative EXTYPE values identify local-enhancement exceptions: this implementation uses -99000, -99001, -99004 and -99993 for its internal errors; when such a value is propagated out of a procedure it becomes -100000 plus the original value (e.g. -100042 for -42). | EXC-0060 |
| 12.1 | D-12.1-2 | core | The precise format of the string that EXTEXT$ returns (Appendix C, subsection 12.1 item 2). | EXTEXT$(n) rounds n to an integer and returns the Table 9 message text in the form description plus parenthesized clause list, e.g. EXTEXT$(1001) is the string Overflow in evaluating numeric-constant (5.1, 15.1); for a number that is not a standard system exception (e.g. 2002) it returns the null string. The real-time codes of Table 9 (1201-1204, 4201-4204, 6301, 12001-12007, 12101-12103, 12201) also return the null string, because the real-time module is not implemented (A-14-01). | EXC-0061 |
| 12.2 | D-12.2-1 | core | What the debugging system allows the user to do at a break point, including how execution continues or ends (Appendix C, subsection 12.2 item 1). | No interactive debugger in the CLI: an uncaught BREAK with debugging active prints a Warning 10007 line report and continues with the next line (exit 0); 10007 is nonfatal and may be caught in a WHEN block, where CONTINUE or RETRY resumes execution. | EXC-0062 |
| 12.2 | D-12.2-2 | core | The exact form of the trace reports (Appendix C, subsection 12.2 item 2). | Each trace report is a single line [TRACE] followed by the line number and the source text of that line, sent to the channel named in TRACE ... TO or to channel zero, e.g. [TRACE] 130 LET A = 42. A TRACE statement without channel-expression also writes 'Trace mode ON'/'Trace mode OFF' on channel zero; with TO #ch the reports go to that file (§12.2.4 l.9132-9136 fixes the destination; only the content is implementation-defined, l.9138) and no mode message is written to channel zero (decision of the project owner, 2026-11-03). The required reports have their own line: a control transfer as [TRACE] A -> B and the assignments of a line as [TRACE] N name=value, with the evaluated subscripts of an array element (C(3)=5), every element of a MAT assignment and string values in quotes; the name is spelled as it appears in the statement that assigns it (LET w = 20 reports w=20; §12.2.4 l.9125-9131). | EXC-0063, EXC-0081, EXC-0082, EXC-0265 |
| 13.1.6 | D-13.1-1 | graphics | How the program selects a particular graphic display device is left to the implementation (Appendix C, subsection 13.1). | One implicit graphics workstation (channel #0); per input class device numbers start at 1 (ASK MAX POINT/MULTIPOINT/CHOICE/VALUE DEVICE = 1,2,3,4); no statement selects a display device. ASK DEVICE SIZE gives 1 1 OTHER and the initial device viewport is 0 1 0 1; there is no pixel reading, so ASK PIXEL SIZE gives 0 0 and ASK PIXEL VALUE -1 (measured with the CLI). | GFX-0117 |
| 13.1.6 | D-13.1-2 | graphics | The effect of a window whose left edge exceeds its right, or whose bottom exceeds its top, is left to the implementation (Appendix C, subsection 13.1). | Inverted window (left>right or bottom>top) accepted without exception; ASK WINDOW returns the values as set (e.g. 2,1,0,1); visual inversion left to the host renderer. | GFX-0118 |
| 13.2.4 | D-13.2-1 | graphics | How many line styles exist is left to the implementation (Appendix C, subsection 13.2). | 4 line styles (ASK MAX LINE STYLE = 4). | GFX-0119 |
| 13.2.4 | D-13.2-2 | graphics | What line styles other than 1, 2, 3 and 4 draw is left to the implementation (Appendix C, subsection 13.2). | None beyond style 4: SET LINE STYLE 5 raises nonfatal 11062 and style stays 1. | GFX-0120 |
| 13.2.4 | D-13.2-3 | graphics | How many point styles exist is left to the implementation (Appendix C, subsection 13.2). | 5 point styles (ASK MAX POINT STYLE = 5). | GFX-0121 |
| 13.2.4 | D-13.2-4 | graphics | What point styles other than 1 through 5 draw is left to the implementation (Appendix C, subsection 13.2). | None beyond style 5: SET POINT STYLE 6 raises nonfatal 11056. | GFX-0122 |
| 13.2.4 | D-13.2-5 | graphics | How many color values exist is left to the implementation (Appendix C, subsection 13.2). | 16 color indices, 0..15 (ASK MAX COLOR = 15). | GFX-0123 |
| 13.2.4 | D-13.2-6 | graphics | Which color each index holds at the start is left to the implementation (Appendix C, subsection 13.2). | No color mix is established at start: ASK COLOR MIX(i) returns 0,0,0 with status 11087 for every index 0..15. | GFX-0124 |
| 13.2.4 | D-13.2-7 | graphics | Whether SET COLOR MIX recolors what is already on screen is left to the implementation (Appendix C, subsection 13.2). | SET COLOR MIX affects only subsequently drawn primitives; the draw log records SET_COLOR_MIX and never recolors logged primitives. | GFX-0125 |
| 13.2.4 | D-13.2-8 | graphics | The color mix values in force at the start of execution are left to the implementation (Appendix C, subsection 13.2). | Initial mixes are unset (as D-13.2-6): every index 0..15 reports status 11087 and zeros. | GFX-0126 |
| 15.1.4 | D-15.1-1 | fixed | The maximum precision P that bounds the decimal digits used to represent numeric values under fixed decimal is chosen by each implementation, but it must be at least 18 digits (Appendix C, subsection 15.1, item 1). | P = 18 decimal digits; FIX-0008 shows an 18-digit integer constant accepted under *18.0 and a 19-digit one raising 1001 | FIX-0008 |
| 15.1.4 | D-15.1-2 | fixed | The precision attribute of the result of evaluating a fixed-decimal numeric expression or numeric supplied function is left to each implementation (Appendix C, subsection 15.1, item 2). | The result of an operation (+, -, *, /) is kept with up to P+2 = 20 significant digits and is not rounded to the default fixed-point-size of the OPTION ARITHMETIC FIXED statement until it is assigned (FIX-0012: in *8.2, LET A = 1/3 stores .33, but the expression 1/3 is .33333333333333333333 and 1/3 = .33 is false). An expression printed as a print item shows the default fixed-point-size of the option (the recommendation of 15.1.6). The numeric supplied functions whose result is always an integer (EXTYPE, EXLINE, INT, IP, CEIL, SGN, LEN, POS, ORD, MAXLEN, MAXSIZE, SIZE, LBOUND, UBOUND, DATE) give a result of fraction-size 0 that prints like a constant: PRINT INT(2.5) prints 2, not 2.00; an expression built on them (INT(2.5) + 1) keeps the default size. Every intermediate result is checked: with A of 16 integer digits under *18.0, A*A/A raises 1002 at A*A although the final result would fit (l.12230-12234; measured with the CLI). | FIX-0012 |
| 15.1.4 | D-15.1-3 | fixed | How accurately a fixed-decimal numeric expression or numeric supplied function is evaluated is left to each implementation (Appendix C, subsection 15.1, item 3). | Operations are computed in decimal with P+2 = 20 significant digits, two more than P, as 15.1.6 recommends, and the operands (constants, variables, intermediate results) keep their own precision (FIX-0013: in *8.2, 1/3*3 is .99999999999999999999, so 1/3*3 = 1 is false, while LET C = 1/3*3 stores 1.00 and 0.1+0.2 = .3 is true; FIX-0174) | FIX-0013 |
| 15.1.4 | D-15.1-4 | fixed | The exact rule for which digits of a constant count as significant is left to each implementation (Appendix C, subsection 15.1, item 4). | Digits as written count as significant: a numeric-constant used as a print item prints exactly those digits, with 17 or 18 integer digits included when P >= 18 (l.12250-12259; FIX-0009/FIX-0015/FIX-0050). As an operand of an expression the constant keeps those digits (1.555 = 1.56 is false); when it is assigned it is rounded to the fixed-point-size of the variable, and when an expression or constant is converted by STR$ the text uses the default fixed-point-size of the program-unit OPTION ARITHMETIC FIXED statement (FIX-0010 verifies this via STR$ in *9.9). A negated constant such as -12345678901234567 is not a numeric-constant in an expression: the sign belongs to the numeric-expression (5.3.2 prod. 2, 'sign? term') and the constant is its primary, so the digits of the result are implementation-defined (l.12250-12259). Here the result is materialized with the default size and limited to P = 18 digits in all: under FIXED*8.2, PRINT -1234567 gives -1234567.00, PRINT -12345678901234567 (17 integer digits) gives -12345678901234567.0 (scale 1) and PRINT -123456789012345678 (18 integer digits) gives -123456789012345678 (scale 0). FIX-0171 pins this. | FIX-0010, FIX-0171 |
| 15.1.4 | D-15.1-5 | fixed | Whether an INTERNAL format file opened under one ARITHMETIC option can be accessed under another is left to each implementation; FIXED with a different default precision still counts as the same option (Appendix C, subsection 15.1, item 5). | INTERNAL files are accessible across different ARITHMETIC options: a datum written under FIXED reads back correctly under DECIMAL (FIX-0016) | FIX-0016 |
| 15.1.4 | D-15.1-6 | fixed | Whether a NATIVE format file opened under one ARITHMETIC option can be accessed under another is left to each implementation (Appendix C, subsection 15.1, item 6). | NATIVE files are accessible across different ARITHMETIC options: a NUMERIC*4.2 field written under FIXED reads back as 12.35 under DECIMAL (FIX-0018) | FIX-0018 |
| 15.1.4 | D-15.1-7 | fixed | The way a value is rounded when it is assigned to a fixed-point variable with fewer fraction digits is not fixed by section 15.1.4, which only says it is rounded. | Half away from zero on the magnitude: LET A = -1.555 stores -1.56 and LET B = 1.555 stores 1.56 under *8.2 (FIX-0178); the same tie-break as the format items of PRINT USING (D-5.4-6). ROUND is different: it follows its normative formula INT(X*10^N+.5)/10^N, so ROUND(-1.555,2) is -1.55. | FIX-0178 |
| 15.2.2 | D-15.2.2-1 | fixed | Whether the ARITHMETIC options of two program-units joined by CHAIN must agree in fixed-point precision or only in type, and whether the numeric parameters of the program-name-line are subject to the ordering rule of OPTION ARITHMETIC FIXED. | Agreed interpretation of 15.2.2 (decision of the project owner, 2026-11-02): 15.2.2 l.12354-12357 only requires the ARITHMETIC options of the two program-units to agree in type (DECIMAL, NATIVE or FIXED), not in precision, so CHAIN from FIXED*4.2 to FIXED*8.2 executes without exception 4303 (SEG-0324); NATIVE vs DECIMAL still raise 4303 both ways (SEG-0311, SEG-0312). The ordering rule of 15.1.2 l.12145-12148 does not reach the parameters of the program-name-line (the first line), so a FIXED program with numeric program parameters is conforming. | SEG-0324, SEG-0311, SEG-0312 |

## 6. Enhancements over the standard

ECMA-116 is a subset of ANSI X3.113-1987 and defines none of the enhancements listed in section 6 of COMPLIANCE_ANSI.md; none is claimed here.

_None._
